science.title: Vision-guided robotic pick-and-place with variable focal length optics: mathematical modelling, illumination optimisation, and sub-millimetre accuracy assessment
science.description: The application of robot-based visual pick-and-place technology entails the simultaneous optimization of optics and lighting systems to ensure sub-millimetre accuracy for high throughput flexible manufacturing processes. This paper explores the development, mathematical modeling, and practical application of a unified framework of a robotic manipulator with a modular machine vision system using interchangeable C-mount lenses over a focal length of 3–35 mm. An analytical model is formulated for the field of view, depth of focus, resolution, and radial distortion of optics. The performance of six lighting modes, namely ambient, low intensity ring LED, high intensity ring LED, dome diffuse, coaxial, and structured light, is compared based on detection ratio, Michelson contrast ratio, and positional error for 4,200 samples. The combined optical-photometric model for performance optimization regarding both focal length and illumination under variable operating conditions is presented. The hand-eye calibration procedure based on the Tsai-Lenz method results in a reprojection error of 0.12 pixels. The RMS error propagation model predicts a total positional uncertainty of 0.450 mm, which compares closely with the experimentally measured value, the 0.090 mm difference being well within the ± 0.19 mm (1σ) positional precision of the system. The optimum (f = 25 mm, structured illumination) yields an accuracy of 0.54 mm in position and 0.76° in orientation, with a precision of ± 0.19 mm (1σ) and a success rate of 98.7% in a validation run of 1,200 placements at the optimal configuration, outperforming the four benchmarked techniques considered in this study.

science.title: An Atomically Dispersed Copper-Catalyst Lights the Way to Selective N-Demethylations
science.description: N-demethylation is a key transformation in drug metabolism, medicinal chemistry, and late-stage amine diversification. Herein, we report a noble-metal-free, recyclable heterogeneous photocatalyst comprising atomically dispersed Cu sites on functionalized graphitic carbon nitride (Cu@f-gC3N4) for selective N-demethylation and N-dealkylation. Under 390 nm irradiation and an oxygen atmosphere, a broad range of tertiary amines, including pharmaceutically relevant substrates, are converted to secondary amines in high yields. The reaction is readily scalable to 10 mmol, and the catalyst retains its activity over more than ten reuse cycles. Atomically isolated Cu sites were confirmed by XPS, ssNMR, STEM, and EXAFS. Mechanistic studies, including radical trapping, isotope labeling, reactive oxygen species detection, kinetic analysis, in situ FTIR, and DFT calculations, support a photoredox pathway involving amine oxidation, superoxide formation, hydrogen abstraction, iminium generation, and hydrolysis, providing a structurally defined and mechanistically understood photocatalytic platform. Herein, the authors present a noble-metal-free, recyclable, and structurally defined heterogeneous photocatalytic platform for selective N-demethylation based on atomically dispersed Cu sites supported on functionalized graphitic carbon nitride.

science.title: Toward the application of blind quantum computing: a case study
science.description: As quantum computing technology matures, an asymmetric computational landscape is emerging where powerful quantum data centers serve users with limited quantum capabilities. The Quantum Internet will enable users to access remote quantum resources, but this delegation raises privacy and trust concerns when the server cannot be assumed to be fully trusted. In this work, we study an implementation-oriented case study in which a Blind Quantum Computing (BQC) protocol is integrated with the encoding stage of a quanvolutional feature extractor for image classification. The goal is to evaluate how an existing BQC-compatible remote state preparation mechanism behaves when used inside a hybrid Quantum Machine Learning workflow. The client encodes classical pixel values as private rotation angles, while fresh random masks hide these angles from an honest-but-curious server at the protocol level. The quantum preprocessing is simulated with finite-shot computational-basis measurements in SquidASM/NetSquid, rather than ideal expectation values, and is evaluated on a small MNIST subset selected for computational feasibility. We analyze the resulting trade-offs among finite-shot sampling, communication and entanglement overhead, depolarizing link and device noise, seed sensitivity, and random-circuit complexity. The study provides practical evidence on the resource and performance constraints that arise when embedding BQC primitives into quantum machine-learning applications, and identifies limitations that must be addressed before deployment-oriented privacy-preserving QML can be considered practical.

ai.title: AI Music Is Growing, But Is India’s Copyright Law Ready?
ai.description: The battle between artificial intelligence (AI) companies and the music industry is widening, with fresh lawsuits and court rulings bringing renewed attention to how AI models are trained, who owns AI-generated music and whether creators are being adequately compensated. The latest action came from independent music publisher Round Hill Music, which sued AI companies Anthropic and Suno in a California federal court, alleging that they misused hundreds of songs controlled by the publisher to train their systems. The cases add to a growing global dispute over copyrighted training data and come as AI-generated music begins moving from an experimental technology into a commercial part of the music ecosystem.
